content: 1. According to national guidelines, follow Algorithm 3 for additional testing. 2. If the patient is not at high risk for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), repeat testing using a molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic (mWRD) with a second sample. The initial instrument output for the result can be reviewed to aid interpretation when available. 3. Low and very low semi-quantitative results have been associated with increased false resistance in some settings. 4. If the second test also indicates rifampicin (RIF) resistance, initiate an MDR/RR-TB treatment regimen in accordance with national guidelines and WHO recommendations, and follow Algorithm 3 for further testing. 5. If the mWRD result for the second sample is MTBC detected, RIF resistance not detected, initiate treatment with a first-line regimen as per national guidelines. False-positive RIF-resistant results due to assay performance are rare but may occur due to laboratory or clerical errors. It is assumed that the repeat test will be performed with greater caution, and the second test result is considered correct. Mixed infections in high-burden settings could also explain such discrepancies, and patients should be closely monitored and retested if their response to first-line treatment is poor. 6. If isoniazid (INH) resistance or susceptibility results are available, interpret and follow up as described in Algorithm 4. 7. If the mWRD result for the second sample is MTBC detected, RIF resistance inconclusive, further investigation is required. A possible mixed infection may explain this scenario. The patient’s history of prior treatment and TB contact history should be reassessed. Management decisions regarding Hr-TB or MDR/RR-TB should be based on further investigations, including phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) for RIF and INH, and DNA sequencing where available. A third mWRD should be performed to decide on initial therapy, and the patient should be closely monitored while awaiting definitive results. The appropriate algorithm should be followed. 8. If a moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) was performed and INH results are also available, this could provide additional certainty. INH resistance is associated with RIF resistance, and the finding of INH resistance should prompt further investigation to exclude RIF resistance. 9. For all patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB, conduct additional investigations to assess resistance to the drugs being used in the treatment regimen. Rapid detection of fluoroquinolone (FQ) resistance is essential for determining the appropriate regimen. The recent addition of a low-complexity automated NAAT for FQ resistance detection provides a rapid and accurate peripheral-level solution that can be performed directly on specimens. 10. Second-line line probe assays (SL-LPA) and DNA sequencing methods are available to evaluate drug resistance beyond RIF and INH. Rapid molecular methods are preferred. However, for resistance detection to new and repurposed drugs, phenotypic DST is currently the only available option, and two separate specimens may be required. 11. MDR/RR-TB regimens rely on the use of FQs. Submit a sample for molecular testing for FQ resistance (see Algorithm 3). Ideally, a specimen from each patient should be submitted for DST for each of the drugs used in the regimen for which reliable testing methods exist. Phenotypic DST can take weeks or even months to provide results. 12. Any positive culture recovered during treatment monitoring that suggests treatment failure should undergo DST for the drugs used in the treatment regimen. 13. If the mWRD gives a result of MTBC detected, RIF indeterminate, the patient will require further investigation. Interpretation and follow-up testing for Xpert Ultra differ from other mWRDs. With any mWRD, the initial result of MTBC detected should be considered bacteriological confirmation of TB. The patient should be initiated on an appropriate regimen using first-line TB drugs in accordance with national guidelines unless the patient is at high risk for MDR-TB, in which case an MDR-TB regimen should be initiated. 14. For most mWRDs, an MTBC detected, RIF resistance indeterminate result is generally caused by a paucibacillary TB load in the sample. In such cases, retesting a fresh specimen is recommended. Testing a second sample, which might also contain very few bacteria, may generate a result of MTBC detected, RIF indeterminate or MTBC not detected. In these situations, additional investigations such as culture, phenotypic DST, molecular testing of the isolate, or sequencing may be needed to confirm or exclude RIF resistance, as the indeterminate result provides no information on resistance. 15. For certain populations, such as people living with HIV (PLHIV) and children being evaluated for pulmonary TB, individuals being evaluated for extrapulmonary TB using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), lymph nodes, and tissue specimens, and adults being evaluated for pulmonary TB who are not at risk for HIV and do not have a history of prior TB treatment within the past five years, initiate the patient on an appropriate regimen using first-line TB drugs in accordance with national guidelines unless the patient is at high risk for MDR-TB. 16. For adults with a history of recent TB treatment or unknown treatment history, consider the possibility of the Xpert Ultra trace result being a false positive due to the presence of non-viable bacilli. Clinically re-evaluate the patient and conduct additional testing (including liquid culture) in accordance with national guidelines. Consider the possibility of TB caused by reactivation, relapse, or reinfection. 17. In initiating treatment, consider the clinical presentation and context of the patient. Make clinical decisions based on all available information and clinical judgment. Further investigations for TB may include chest X-ray, additional clinical assessments, and clinical response following treatment with broad-spectrum antimicrobial agents (fluoroquinolones should not be used). 18. Repeat Xpert Ultra testing is of uncertain benefit. A recent WHO guideline development group recommended against repeat Xpert Ultra testing for individuals with an initial Xpert Ultra trace result for the detection of MTBC. Culture and phenotypic DST may be of benefit to detect TB and drug resistance. The trace result provides no information on RIF resistance. 19. If the mWRD does not give a result or gives a result of error or invalid, repeat the mWRD at the same testing site with a second specimen. 20. Discordant results may occur, usually when comparing culture-based results with molecular results. Each discordant result will need to be investigated on a case-by-case basis. General considerations include using the mWRD result and clinical judgment to guide treatment decisions pending additional testing.
